Thank you for submitting your article "Neural activity in corticobasal ganglia circuits of juvenile songbirds encodes performance during goal-directed learning" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom, Ronald L Calabrese (Reviewer #1), is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen Andrew King as the Senior Editor. We had two new referees.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission. Given that this paper has gone through two full rounds of review and remains in an unacceptable form, we are prepared to offer only one more opportunity to provide an acceptable version of the manuscript.

Summary:

This interesting manuscript compares the properties and developmental changes of neuronal activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits of the zebra finch during the juvenile song leaning period. During this period, juvenile songbirds are actively engaged in evaluating feedback of self-generated behavior in relation to their memorized tutor song (the goal). This work focuses on the well-studied cortical LMAN CORE and on the surrounding SHELL, which the corresponding author's group has delineated in several previous studied and implicated in the process of learning during song development of juveniles. It also tracks development of songs themselves during this period of song learning so that neuronal responses and songs can be compared as learning progresses. The paper uses sophisticated analyses of songs and of responses of CORE and SHELL neurons recorded in awake singing juvenile birds, which present a consistent picture. The spiking patterns of a subset neurons in both SHELL and CORE reflect the degree of tutor song matching during singing. Both CORE and SHELL neurons encode tutor similarity either by increases or decreases in firing rate, but only SHELL neurons showed a significant association at the population level. During development, tutor similarity (for syllables with low initial similarity to tutor syllables) predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and SHELL but not CORE neurons showed decreases in response variability, suggesting that the activity of SHELL neurons reflects the progression of learning. These results suggest that individual LMAN neurons may function to compare sensory feedback and efference copy from current motor actions, with Shell serving as the critic and CORE as the actor.

Essential revisions:

This paper was difficult to read because the analyses are complicated and somewhat abstract, and many separate issues are addressed which are peripheral to the main interest of the paper; during development, tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and SHELL but not CORE neurons showed decreases in response variability. This paper has thus much inherent interest but is too unwieldly as presented and how it should be revised was the subject of lively constructive discussion by the expert reviewers. In revision, the authors should focus and provide detailed responses to the points below.

1) The main revision must be to simplify the message of the paper by focusing ONLY on the song similarity analysis.a) The 'premotor vs non premotor' analyses are not necessary to support the main finding, and given the relatively weak support in favor of a CORE-SHELL distinction on that issue, it should be removed.b) A large portion of the results is devoted to showing that juvenile syllables become more and more similar to tutor during early song development. Although previous studies have focused on the later stages of learning, song similarity is known to increase even in the early stages of learning (e.g. Aronov et al., 2008). The authors should cut substantially the lengthy description and analysis of song development to concentrate on the core issues; during development, tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and SHELL but not CORE neurons showed decreases in response variability.c) The concentration on the relation between LMAN firing and the acoustic properties of the syllables is unwarranted. The issue here is that findings are very weak. The authors make a very problematic statistical claim about representation of multiple features but no single feature. This could be, in principle, true, but the analyses show simply a very weak effect, as opposed to synergy or gestalt representation. It is not possible to see anything interesting in the raw data. To quote one of the expert reviewers in discussion "The entire section about analysis of acoustic features, and all figures showing nothing apparent, should be removed, and replaced by something like "we found a very weak, but statistically significant representation of song features (t=… p=… see suppl.)."d) Another issue that undermines the clarity of the paper is the intermixing of results that apply both to LMAN-core and LMAN-shell neurons and results that contrast between these two areas. The authors should highlight similarities and differences between these two areas. As suggested by the first sentence in the discussion, the main finding of the paper applies to both core and shell neurons, and only minor differences are found between the singing-related firing in these two populations. This could be made more explicit throughout the results.

[Editors' note: further revisions were requested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Neural activity in corticobasal ganglia circuits of juvenile songbirds encodes performance during goal-directed learning" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Andrew King (Senior editor), a Reviewing editor, and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

The manuscript is much improved and all comments were fully addressed.

There are two remaining issues that should be resolved before this paper is published.

1) Regressions of baseline-corrected firing rates against tutor similarity for each neuron revealed that cells in both CORE and SHELL exhibited either positive or negative associations between neural activity and degree of tutor similarity: approximately half of all neurons in each subregion showed positive slopes (r values > 0, increased firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity).

We should have noticed this issue in the previous round, but this description is deficient. Saying that half increased and half decreased is like looking at random data, right? Instead, plot a histogram of all those slopes and/or r values, so readers can see the distribution on both positive and negative sides. Then do bootstrap (shuffling tutor similarity) to plot this histogram against a random distribution of similarities. This way, it would be possible to evaluate if this is a real correlation.

2) Response strength did not differ between CORE and SHELL neurons for either excitation or suppression (Table 1; Mann-Whitney tests: singing-excited neurons U = 1768, p = 0.06, singing-suppressed neurons U = 459, p = 0.90).

Maybe you should not say that there is no difference for singing excited neurons since 0.06 is almost significant. Instead, say that you see a borderline difference between core and shell, which did not reach significance level, for song-excited neurons, but no apparent effect in the song-suppressed neurons and then give the p values.

If the statistical tests in comment #1 work out satisfactorily, then further review by the expert reviewers will not be required.

claims.claim: The relationship between firing rates and tutor similarity in shell neurons does not appear to be based on prototypicality of self-generated syllables.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the scatter of syllable renditions within a syllable type between the high- and low-similarity to tutor categories.

claims.claim: Variability in firing rate was higher across the populations of both core and shell neurons during production of syllable renditions with low tutor similarity compared to production of syllable renditions with high tutor similarity.

claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the CV analysis.

claims.claim: The developmental span over which birds were recorded (43–60 dph) corresponds with a transition from highly variable 'subsong' to 'plastic song' with less behavioral variability and a corresponding increase in similarity to tutor song.

claims.claim: Comparing degree of song development with acoustic similarity to tutor across average syllable types yielded a significant correlation.

claims.claim: Juvenile birds produce syllable renditions that are more similar to tutor syllables as sensorimotor integration progresses.

claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the current data.

claims.claim: Birds produced many utterances with relatively high tutor similarity during subsong.

claims.claim: Some of the highly variable vocalizations produced by birds during early sensorimotor learning are good matches to tutor syllables.

claims.claim: The similarity between poorly-matched renditions and tutor syllables increased as song development progressed.
claims.source: Birds in subsong also produced many low-similarity utterances (Figure 7B, left), and the similarity between these poorly-matched renditions and tutor syllables increased as song development progressed, reflecting the expected increase in tutor matching (r = 0.34, p=0.03; cf. Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Birds in subsong produce some utterances with tutor similarity as high as that of birds in later stages of song development, and renditions with lower tutor similarity at the beginning of sensorimotor integration are gradually eliminated.

claims.claim: The syllable type that was produced most frequently in the high-similarity category was also produced most frequently in the low-similarity category in 57% of vocal recording sessions across all birds.
claims.source: We examined whether individual syllable types were selectively represented in high- versus low-similarity categories for each day of singing, and found that the syllable type that was produced most frequently in the high-similarity category (highest percentage of renditions among all syllable types) was also produced most frequently in the low-similarity category. The most common syllable type produced was the same for both high- and low-similarity renditions in 57% of vocal recording sessions across all birds, indicating that a single syllable type did not typically predominate in either low- or high- similarity categories.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of syllable type distributions in high- and low-similarity categories.

claims.claim: Syllable renditions within both high- and low-similarity categories represent multiple syllable types.
claims.source: This pattern is consistent with the finding above that syllable renditions within both high- and low-similarity categories represent multiple syllable types (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: Absolute values of response strength across song development increased in both core and shell neurons regardless of whether syllable renditions had high or low similarity to tutor syllables.

claims.claim: Both core and shell neurons showed stronger associations between firing rate and tutor similarity during early stages of song development, and weaker associations as sensorimotor learning progressed.
claims.source: Both core and shell neurons showed stronger associations between firing rate and tutor similarity during early stages of song development, and weaker associations as sensorimotor learning progressed.

claims.claim: CV of firing rate in shell neurons decreased over the course of song development only during production of syllable renditions that had low similarity to tutor during early sensorimotor learning.

claims.claim: Variability of firing in shell neurons did not change for utterances with high similarity to tutor song across development.

claims.claim: The variability of firing in shell neurons reflected the progression of learning, with higher neural variability early in development for renditions with lower similarity to tutor song, and lower neural variability later in development as the incidence of poorly-matched syllable renditions decreased.

claims.claim: Neurons in both core and shell subregions of LMAN showed singing-related activity that varied as a function of tutor song similarity during early stages of sensorimotor integration.

claims.claim: This pattern represents the first discovery of an online correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds.
claims.source: This pattern represents the first discovery of an online correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds and suggests LMAN as a key component of circuitry that evaluates current behavior in relation to a goal behavior during procedural learning.

claims.claim: LMAN is a key component of circuitry that evaluates current behavior in relation to a goal behavior during procedural learning.

claims.claim: Although neural activity across the population in both core and shell was modulated by degree of similarity between self-generated sounds and memorized tutor sounds, this trend was stronger across the population of shell neurons.

claims.claim: Spiking activity in core neurons supports the idea that core drives vocal motor output in juvenile birds.

claims.claim: Shell circuitry acts primarily as a 'critic' to evaluate comparisons between self-generated and tutor sounds, while core circuitry serves as an 'actor' that drives vocal motor output and receives instruction from the critic in order to bias action selection over the course of learning.

claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results, supported by citations to actor-critic models.

claims.claim: Some individual syllable renditions were similar to tutor syllables even in subsong birds during early sensorimotor integration, indicating a surprising capacity to produce relatively mature syllabic utterances.

claims.claim: This result is reminiscent of the finding that juvenile birds exposed to adult females are able to produce more stereotyped song patterns than normally seen in young birds.

results.result: Core and shell subregions of LMAN form parallel cortico-basal ganglia loops with distinct functional roles: core mediates vocal motor production while shell evaluates sensorimotor learning without causing motor disruption when lesioned.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 establish the anatomical organization and functional dissociation between core and shell pathways through citations to prior anatomical studies and lesion experiments (C15, C119-C120). The lesion data showing impaired learning but preserved motor function provides strong evidence for the evaluative role of shell circuitry.

results.result: Neural activity in both core and shell LMAN neurons during singing correlates with acoustic similarity to tutor syllables, with neurons encoding tutor similarity via either increases or decreases in firing rate. Shell neurons show a significant population-level association (p=0.035) while core neurons do not (p=0.37).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C36-C44, and C71-C74 present converging evidence from single-neuron correlations, permutation tests, and mixed-effects regression analyses. The statistical analyses are appropriate and the finding that ~50% of neurons show positive correlations while ~50% show negative correlations (C36-C37) is well-documented. The population-level significance in shell but not core (C41-C42) is supported by proper statistical testing.

results.result: The majority of neurons in both core and shell show significant modulation during singing, with approximately 65-70% showing excitation and the remainder suppressed. Basic profiles of neural activity during song production are similar between core and shell.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 describe fundamental electrophysiological properties supported by data in Table 1 and Figures 2-3. The statistical comparisons between core and shell are appropriate (Mann-Whitney tests), and the findings are consistent with prior literature (C28, C30 cite previous work).

results.result: Core neurons show coordinated premotor increases in firing rate prior to syllable onsets, while shell neurons lack time-locked premotor activity, consistent with core driving vocal motor output and shell having a non-motor evaluative role.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 and C75-C76 are supported by population histogram analyses (Figure 3) showing significant premotor activity in core but not shell. This pattern is consistent with anatomical projections and lesion data (C76 cites supporting evidence), providing converging support for the functional dissociation.

results.result: Both core and shell neurons show increased firing rate variability (CV) during production of syllables with low tutor similarity compared to high similarity (p<0.001 for both), and this difference is not explained by differences in syllable type composition or scatter.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by statistical analyses (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) and control analyses ruling out confounds related to syllable type diversity (C49-C50). The CV analysis is appropriate for assessing neural variability and the controls strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: Juvenile birds produce syllables with high tutor similarity even during subsong, with these high-similarity utterances remaining constant across development (r=0.13, p=0.42), while low-similarity utterances progressively improve (r=0.34, p=0.03).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 present a novel behavioral finding supported by correlation analyses across development. The statistical tests are appropriate and the finding that subsong birds can produce mature-sounding syllables (C55-C57) is surprising but well-documented with quantitative data (Figure 7B).

results.result: The correlation between firing rate and tutor similarity decreases as learning progresses in both core and shell neurons, with tutor similarity being a better predictor of firing rate during early learning when behavioral variability is high.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C86-C88 are supported by developmental correlation analyses (Figure 8) showing weakening associations between neural activity and tutor similarity as song matures. This pattern is consistent with the loss of tutor-tuned neurons (C87) and provides insight into changing neural mechanisms across learning.

results.result: CV of firing rate in shell neurons decreases across development for low-similarity syllables (r=-0.24, p=0.01) but not high-similarity syllables (r=-0.08, p=0.42), while core neuron CV shows no developmental changes regardless of tutor similarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 and C82-C85 demonstrate that shell but not core neurons track learning progression through changes in firing variability. The correlation analyses are appropriate and the selective developmental change in shell for low-similarity syllables (C67) provides strong evidence that shell activity reflects learning progression.

results.result: The association between firing rate and tutor similarity in shell neurons is not explained by encoding of syllable prototypicality (t=-1.53, p=0.136).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 present an important control analysis using mixed-effects regression to rule out an alternative explanation. The statistical test is appropriate and the negative result strengthens the interpretation that shell neurons specifically encode tutor similarity rather than general syllable quality.

results.result: Shell neurons show selective responses to either tutor song or own song during playback, with ~30% responding specifically to tutor song. This tutor-tuned population is transient and disappears by late learning stages. Core neurons respond to own song or both song types but rarely to tutor song alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 and C121-C128 describe playback response properties supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior work (C17). The finding of selective tutor-tuned neurons in shell (C125) and their developmental loss (C22, C127) is well-documented, though the mechanism (cell death vs. retuning, C128) remains speculative.

results.result: Shell circuitry acts as a 'critic' to evaluate comparisons between self-generated and tutor sounds, while core serves as an 'actor' driving vocal motor output and receiving instruction from the critic.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 presents an actor-critic interpretation of the data with citations to relevant models (Barto et al., 1983; Graybiel, 2008). While the functional dissociation between shell and core is well-supported, the specific claim that shell instructs core requires additional experiments (e.g., manipulations showing causal influence) that are not presented in this study.

results.result: Positive correlations between firing rate and tutor similarity may provide reinforcement signals, while negative correlations may provide error signals, with both types of information potentially guiding syllable refinement.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 present speculative interpretations of the functional significance of bidirectional encoding. While the observation of both positive and negative correlations is well-supported, the specific functional roles (reinforcement vs. error signals) require additional experiments (e.g., manipulations, downstream recordings) to validate.

results.result: Core neurons in juveniles, but not adults, send transient axon collaterals into the shell pathway (AId), potentially conveying corollary discharge signals and providing integration between pathways during learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 and C129-C132 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and citations to prior work (Miller-Sims and Bottjer, 2012). The developmental specificity is well-documented, though the functional interpretation as corollary discharge (C97, C132) is somewhat speculative but reasonable given the anatomical and lesion evidence.

results.result: The functional organization of core and shell pathways parallels mammalian sensorimotor and associative cortico-basal ganglia loops, with associative circuits (shell) showing early engagement that decreases with learning while sensorimotor circuits (core) remain engaged.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 draw comparisons to mammalian literature supported by extensive citations (C105). The parallel between shell/core and associative/sensorimotor loops is reasonable given the anatomical organization and the developmental patterns observed (declining shell variability, C108), though direct homology claims would require additional comparative evidence.

results.result: This study represents the first discovery of an online neural correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 asserts novelty but does not provide systematic comparison to prior literature to establish this is truly the first such finding. While the specific finding of tutor similarity encoding during singing in juveniles may be novel, the claim requires more thorough documentation of what has been shown previously to be fully evaluated.

results.result: Birds may switch from comparing utterances to a tutor template to a self template as learning progresses, with tutor-tuned neurons potentially acting as a gate or filter for tutor-similar utterances during early learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 present speculative interpretations about changing learning strategies. While the developmental changes in tutor-tuned neurons and increasing own-song selectivity (C90, supported by citations) are documented, the specific mechanisms of template switching and gating functions require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: Developmental changes in LMAN circuitry, including cell death of tutor-tuned neurons, development of topographic specificity, and elimination of silent synapses, may causally contribute to goal-oriented learning and help close the sensitive period.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 discuss developmental mechanisms supported by citations to prior work, but the causal relationships proposed are speculative. While the developmental changes are documented (C100-C101 cite supporting studies), establishing causal links to learning and sensitive period closure (C99, C102-C103) would require manipulative experiments not presented here.
